title: Surface Area of Prisms and Cylinders

findings.finding: The net's front/back and side labels conflict with the solid's orientation and the response scaffold.
findings.breakdown: Following the net gives front/back dimensions 5×2, while following the solid gives 3×2. Both routes produce the same total, concealing the conflicting face correspondence.
findings.checked: Compared the complete solid, labelled net and scaffold in p6-q2-b with the consistent correspondence in p5-example-block and p6-q2-a.
findings.assumptions: The paired representations are intended to retain the same named faces, as in the preceding example.

repair.proposal: Relabel the net's two 5×2 rectangles as sides and its two 3×2 flaps as front and back.

findings.doneWhen: Each named face pair has the same dimensions in the solid, net and response scaffold.

findings.finding: The requested numerical surface area cannot be determined because the prism's height is missing.
findings.breakdown: The equality marks establish a square base of side 8.2 m, but neither a height nor an equality connecting height to a base edge is given. The surface area remains 134.48 + 32.8h square metres.
findings.checked: Compared p10-q4-a's complete givens with the three dimensions used in p8-example-face-pairs-block and supplied in p9-q3-b. No instruction identifies this as an insufficient-information question.
findings.assumptions: The instruction requests a numerical calculation, consistent with the surrounding exercise.

repair.proposal: Supply the intended height. If the intended solid is a cube, add: “This prism is a cube.”

findings.doneWhen: The student-visible givens determine all three dimensions.

findings.finding: Extend the stack comparison to quantify how contact area changes exposed surface area.
findings.breakdown: This develops the existing explanation by comparing two numerical arrangements of the same solids.
findings.checked: Each prism has surface area 321 cm². The original stack has area 963−4(108)=531 cm²; joining on 12×2.5 faces gives 963−4(30)=843 cm². Both calculations use rectangular-prism methods already taught.
findings.assumptions: Each stack has aligned, fully touching faces.

repair.proposal: After Question 6, add optional parts: (a) Calculate the surface area of the stack shown. [531 cm²] (b) Stack the three prisms with their 12 cm × 2.5 cm faces touching. Calculate the new surface area. [843 cm²] (c) Which stack has the smaller surface area? Explain why. [The original stack; its larger touching faces conceal more area.]

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up retains the original solids and compares the two contact-face areas.

findings.finding: The triangular-prism example uses triangle area without an opening review of that substantial prerequisite.
findings.breakdown: Students must calculate one triangular area before combining the identical ends. A recall gap concerning the division by two obstructs that step.
findings.checked: Triangle area appears in p5-guided-components and p7-d/p7-e, but the intervening rectangular-prisms topic and its supplied exercise do not rehearse it. No review precedes p14-example-block.
findings.assumptions: Triangle area is prior knowledge. Calculator availability does not affect formula recall.

repair.proposal: Before p14-example-block, add three short items: (a) Find the area of a triangle with base 8 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm. [20 cm²] (b) Find the area of a triangle with base 7 m and perpendicular height 6 m. [21 m²] (c) Two identical triangular faces each have base 10 mm and perpendicular height 3 mm. Find their combined area. [30 mm²]

findings.doneWhen: A short opening review rehearses triangle area before its use in the worked example.

findings.finding: The cylinder net uses circumference without first rehearsing recall of that circle formula.
findings.breakdown: Students who cannot recall circumference must accept the supplied 2πr label without recovering the prior circle knowledge connecting it to the rectangle's length.
findings.checked: Earlier topics concern polygonal faces. p18-circle-area-cloze rehearses circle area, but the circumference expression is already displayed beside p18-rectangle-dimensions-cloze. Removed radius-versus-diameter conversion from this finding because the worked example supplies a radius directly; conversion first occurs in guided practice.
findings.assumptions: Circumference is previously learned circle knowledge. No calculator assumption is needed for these exact answers.

repair.proposal: Before p18-net-definition, add: (a) Find the circumference of a circle of radius 3 cm, in terms of π. [6π cm] (b) Find the circumference of a circle of radius 5 m, in terms of π. [10π m] (c) Find the circumference of a circle of radius 8 mm, in terms of π. [16π mm] Keep the review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students recall circumference independently before the net uses it as the rectangle's length.

findings.finding: A constant-radius run can expose the fixed contribution of the circular ends and the changing contribution of height.
findings.breakdown: Only height varies through the run; an unpatterned item follows it.
findings.checked: Using A=2πr²+2πrh gives 30π, 42π, 54π and 66π cm² for the run, and 120π cm² for the final item. All stated one-decimal-place answers are correct. The supplied practice has no existing constant-radius run.
findings.assumptions: Use a calculator and retain the existing rounding instruction.

repair.proposal: After p20-q2-f, add one instruction: “Predict how the surface area will change before calculating.” Add further parts under the existing instruction: (g) radius 3 cm, height 2 cm [94.2 cm²]; (h) radius 3 cm, height 4 cm [131.9 cm²]; (i) radius 3 cm, height 6 cm [169.6 cm²]; (j) radius 3 cm, height 8 cm [207.3 cm²]; then (k) diameter 10 cm, height 7 cm [377.0 cm²].

findings.doneWhen: The run holds radius fixed while increasing height by 2 cm, followed by the unpatterned item.

findings.finding: The example uses a rectangle width of 12 cm without deriving it from the labelled radius of 6 cm.
findings.breakdown: Recognising that the cut face spans the diameter is an unwritten geometric decision preceding the multiplication.
findings.checked: p25-d introduces the cut rectangle symbolically, but no student-visible numerical connecting step derives the 12 used in p26-example-top-component. Earlier radius/diameter work does not supply this example's missing line.
findings.assumptions: The worked example must explicitly connect an unlabelled substituted dimension to the given measurement. Calculator availability is irrelevant.

repair.proposal: Before 15×12, add: “The top rectangle's width is the diameter: d = 2r = 2×6 = 12 cm.”

findings.doneWhen: The working derives 12 cm and identifies it as the cut rectangle's width.

findings.finding: Extend the packaging comparison by doubling length and comparing the resulting cardboard saving.
findings.breakdown: The comparison separates the changing side-area saving from the unchanged saving at the ends.
findings.checked: For length 40 cm, the rectangular box has area 672 cm² and the cylinder 168π cm², giving approximately 144 cm² saved. The original saving is 352−88π cm²; twice that is approximately 151 cm². Only previously taught area methods are needed.
findings.assumptions: Both boxes remain closed and snug, with flaps and overlaps ignored as in the original question.

repair.proposal: After the existing task, add optional parts: (b) The same biscuits are packed in boxes 40 cm long. How much cardboard does the cylindrical box save, to the nearest square centimetre? [672−168π ≈ 144 cm²] (c) Is this twice the saving for the 20 cm boxes? Explain why. [No. Doubling length doubles the side-area saving, while the saving at the two ends remains unchanged; twice the original unrounded saving is approximately 151 cm².]

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up uses the existing packaging context and compares savings without premature rounding.

findings.finding: The example substitutes radius 3 cm without connecting it to the labelled width of 6 cm.
findings.breakdown: Students must identify the roof diameter as the prism width and halve it before either circular calculation. Both calculations omit that decision.
findings.checked: p30-example-solid supplies width 6 cm; both circular components use 3. Earlier teaching supplies the radius–diameter relationship but does not state this example's numerical conversion.
findings.assumptions: The example must explicitly derive an unlabelled dimension used in its working. Calculator availability is irrelevant.

repair.proposal: Before the component calculations, add: “The roof diameter is 6 cm, so r = 6÷2 = 3 cm.”

findings.doneWhen: One connecting line derives the radius used in both circular calculations.

findings.finding: The tunnel questions introduce exposed internal walls without showing how they differ from concealed joining faces.
findings.breakdown: Students must both subtract the openings and include four tunnel walls. Earlier composite-solid examples exclude internal contact faces, creating a substantial risk of excluding the tunnel walls as well.
findings.checked: p25-cylinder-guidance-block addresses exposed cuts and open ends; p30-example-decomposition, p35-decomposition-block and p36-b address concealed joins. None explicitly treats a through-tunnel's exposed internal walls. The supplied earlier teaching is complete.
findings.assumptions: Students know the required rectangle and cylinder area methods; the unsupported component is identifying exposed tunnel surfaces.

repair.proposal: Before p38-part-e, add: “The four tunnel walls are exposed surfaces, so include their areas. Subtract the rectangular opening from each end face.” Leave dimensions, calculations and totals to students.

findings.doneWhen: Students are explicitly told to include exposed tunnel walls while excluding the two openings before completing either tunnel question.

findings.finding: Extend the attached-cube question by comparing relocation with separation.
findings.breakdown: The comparison distinguishes the position of a fully attached cube from the area concealed at its contact face.
findings.checked: The lower prism has area 992 cm² and the cube 54 cm². Full attachment conceals 18 cm², giving 1028 cm² regardless of position; separation gives 1046 cm². These methods are taught in p35 and p36.
findings.assumptions: The cube's full 3×3 cm base remains attached when moved, without overhanging.

repair.proposal: Immediately after p37-q2-b, add optional parts: (i) Move the 3 cm cube to a corner of the top face, keeping its whole base attached. What is the total surface area? [1028 cm²] (ii) Lift the cube clear of the prism. What is the combined surface area of the two separate solids? [1046 cm²] (iii) Explain why separating them increases the area by 18 cm². [Two previously concealed 3×3 cm faces become exposed.]

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up compares full attachment with separation using the original dimensions.

protectedGroups.observation: The same solid can have nets with its triangular ends attached to different rectangles.
protectedGroups.varies: The attachment position of the two triangular ends.
protectedGroups.invariant: The triangular end shapes, three rectangular lateral faces and resulting triangular prism.

protectedGroups.observation: Different triangle shapes and net arrangements still produce triangular prisms.
protectedGroups.varies: Triangle shape and arrangement of the rectangular faces.
protectedGroups.invariant: Two matching triangular ends joined by three rectangles.

protectedGroups.observation: The multiplication templates fade while students retain the same face-family organisation.
protectedGroups.varies: The amount of supplied working and the numerical dimensions.
protectedGroups.invariant: Three rectangular face pairs are calculated and added.

protectedGroups.observation: Students repeat the inverse surface-area method with the unknown dimension in a different orientation.
protectedGroups.varies: Dimensions, units and position of the unknown edge.
protectedGroups.invariant: Two known dimensions and one unknown dimension yield a linear equation.

protectedGroups.observation: The sequence distinguishes finding a hypotenuse from finding a shorter side before combining either with surface area.
protectedGroups.varies: Which right-triangle side is unknown, dimensions and orientation.
protectedGroups.invariant: A right-triangular cross-section and the sum of two triangular and three rectangular face areas.

protectedGroups.observation: The sequence develops the half-base construction, changes the unknown from sloping side to altitude, then removes the drawn altitude.
protectedGroups.varies: The unknown length and the amount of construction support.
protectedGroups.invariant: An isosceles cross-section whose altitude bisects its base.

protectedGroups.observation: Opening ends removes circular areas while leaving curved area unchanged.
protectedGroups.varies: Two, one or no circular ends.
protectedGroups.invariant: Radius r, height h and the full curved surface.

protectedGroups.observation: Removing the cut-face rectangle and then one end changes only the corresponding surface components.
protectedGroups.varies: Presence of the top rectangle and number of semicircular ends.
protectedGroups.invariant: Radius r, height h and the half-cylinder curved surface.

protectedGroups.observation: The same three-component area sum applies to a net and to cylinders in different orientations, including when only one end area is labelled.
protectedGroups.varies: Representation, orientation and whether both circular areas are explicitly labelled.
protectedGroups.invariant: Two equal circular areas plus one curved-surface area.

protectedGroups.observation: A 10% increase in height produces a smaller percentage increase in total surface area.
protectedGroups.varies: Height and consequently curved surface area.
protectedGroups.invariant: Radius and the combined area of the circular ends.

protectedGroups.observation: Recovering the diameter from an axial-section triangle uses the same method across orientations and numerical forms.
protectedGroups.varies: Orientation and integer, irrational or decimal-derived diameter.
protectedGroups.invariant: Pythagoras gives diameter, which must be halved before applying the surface-area formula.
